maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
To keep peace in the family, Mr. Speaker, after seeing my hon.
friend's hands I withdraw any implication I might have made against him. However, I think I am entitled to make my speech without these interruptions-although, mind you,
I enjoy them.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: So do we.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I am not like some people who can dish it out but can't take it. I enjoy it. But I do say this, Mr. Speaker, by the very nature of things we must in every way possible protect these people who are coming from Europe. I believe that every province in Canada with the exception of Prince Edward Island has fair wage laws. The order in council which permitted these girls to enter the province of Quebec and work in Beauce recognizes the jurisdiction of these minimum wage laws.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Will the minister permit a question about the order in council?

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I ask the question only for the purpose of obtaining information. On April 1, 1947, an order in council, P.C. 1193, was passed on the recommendation of the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen):
. . . that as there is a shortage of textile workers in Canada, the provisions of order in council P.C. 695, dated March 24, 1931, ... be waived in behalf of one hundred immigrants as herein described.
Those are the one hundred textile workers. It has been stated that similar applications have been made by other industrial concerns. Has any other order in council been passed waiving the order in council of 1931 which would deny these persons admission to Canada?

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: The answer is no.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: That is the last one?

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: And the only order in council?

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: As far as I know. I am almost convinced of it, but I will say it is the only one as far as my memory' serves me, if my hon. friend will accept that for now.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: There has not been one since April 1?

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I am not trying to mislead my friend; not intentionally', anyway. To get back to my argument, as I say the girls in question are being brought to Canada within the four corners of our immigration legislation. As the order in council states,
Labour Conditions

the prevailing rates of wages, as laid down by the minimum wage laws of the province of Quebec, will apply; and as I believe I indicated a short while ago every province of Canada with the exception of Prince Edward Island has legislation of that description. It may be unfortunate that it has become necessary, as they have found in Great Britain, to move people from these displaced persons camps in groups. No one knows the difficulties and complications of an undertaking of that kind. The emotions of people from one end of this country to the other are aroused by such a policy. That is inescapable, but I am convinced that these girls certainly have found a better home in Beauce that they had in Germany. It was my privilege to visit those parts of Europe in peace time, and I know something of the conditions that existed in eastern Europe at that time. Yesterday, I think it was, one of these girls told a newspaper man she had a varicose vein caused by pulling a plough. Women do not do those things in any province of Canada, to my knowledge; nor do they do those things on the continent of North America. By the pictures this morning I noticed that these girls were well dressed, and I understand the clothing was provided by their employer.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: The men won't even push a plough.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
That may be true, too.
I do believe, Mr. Speaker, that we are under an obligation to pull our weight on the oar in connection with the movement of these displaced persons from Europe. Let me say . also that people of my own blood are concerned about immigration into this country of people of British stock. At the moment the door is wide open; let us be frank and honest about that. Let us not throw out a smoke-screen in connection with these unfortunate people by suggesting that we are treating one race in one way and another race in another. All they have to do is get passage from Great Britain, and provided they are healthy they can come to Canada. The same applies to South Africa, Australia, New' Zealand and the United States; and I think the country should know that. When you begin to move people, however, there is always objection. When you move the Poles, some other racial group objects. When you move tlie Jews, some other racial group says, "We should not have Jews in this country." When you move the Ukrainians or any other European group, somebody in this dominion, under a free press and freedom of speech, will take objection. I believe we have to be big about this thing, that we must be humane about it, 
and take these people out of real slavery and let. them be absorbed an l assimilated into the life of this dominion. That is what, my hon. friend urged at the united nations. I know quite well that if he w'ere in charge of the immigration policy of this country there would be people who would criticize, from their own points of view', any policy he might set in motion. I have had many wires, as all members and ministers get wires, in connection with the movement of these displaced persons to this country. They are all couched in the same language; and those of us who understand the labour movement know something about the phraseology used by these people who think anyone who is not a communist is a fascist; and that goes for every party in this house. If our judgment is to be influenced by such people, how are we to fashion an immigration policj'?
I hope that when the history of this movement of this year and next year is reviewed we may find that these Polish soldiers who fought so nobly on the side of the allies during the war have been absorbed into the life of this country; and that goes for all the displaced persons that we are ready to receive into our family circle. So let us argue it on that basis. Let us argue from a humanitarian point of view and get it on that plane, so that after the years have rolled by these people. like tens of thousands of others in Canada, will be able to say they are glad they came here and worked their way and raised and educated their families.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: And didn't grouse about the country all the time, either.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Of course not. I am
not unmindful of the forces in this and every other democratic country, whether it be Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Great Britain or the United States, that are working to create confusion of the worst kind. Those of us who have been raised in that atmosphere know something about it.. So today I would ask hon. members to suspend judgment in the case of the member for Beauce until he is here to answer for himself in this high court of parliament. I do not know the hon. member intimately, but I have spoken to him and he always struck me as a kindly person, as a high type of Canadian. Viewed in the light of conditions as they exist at the moment, his judgment and our judgment may have been shortsighted; I don't know.
I do not believe it was, but we should not take a short, view of this thing. Let us wait a year or two and see the position of these girls in our society at that time. For goodness sake don't throw cold water on every English-

Labour Conditions
man, Irishman and Scotsman who wants to come to Canada, or on every Jew, every Ukrainian, every Pole or other European who wants to come to this country. Let us be big and broad about this question of immigration. I believe the vast majority of the people of Canada want to assume all their obligations in connection with these displaced persons in Europe.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has spoken about the lumber operators. Let me tell him that there will be immigration officials and officials of my own to do the screening. That has already been arranged. Let me say this, too-and I have said it before-that nothing my department will do will consciously endanger the wage standards of Canadian workingmen.
I know some of those people at the head of the lakes who have been making statements in the last few days. They are not members of the Progressive Conservative party; they are not members of the C.C.F.; they are not members of the Social Credit party or of the Liberal party. They are members of another party. Perhaps that is some indication why these Polish people and people from other countries in Europe do not want to go back to the place from which they came. The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka) knows about the Ukrainians; he knows that people from Germany do not want to go back to the place they came from. He knows it, and every hon. member in the house knows it. No; they want to come here where there is a measure of real freedom, notwithstanding the expression of opinion of any member of the House of Commons or any person in Canada. They want to come here where there is an opportunity to live their lives in an atmosphere of freedom- freedom of religion, freedom of the press, freedom of assembly, those great freedoms which have made this country what it is.
I would ask in conclusion that we suspend judgment on the hon. member for Beauce until he has had his day in court.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few worda with respect to the motion before the house; and in doing so let me say at the outset that I speak for myself only.
If my memory serves me correctly the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), the leader of the C.C.F., has not so far risen in his place and spoken on the subject of immigration. I presume he felt that that question was too dangerous politically to tackle

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: No.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: -from whatever side you take it, so he delegated some of the lesser lights in his group to take up this question. Of course he was just watching the developments.	*

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. First of all, I did speak on immigration. And may I say this, that this is not a one-man party, and when one of this group leads off on a particular topic he speaks for all of us, myself included. But I spoke on it. Let me say again that this is not a one-man party.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: It is true that the leader of a group has the right to assign certain topics to his followers; but what I would point out is that the leader of the C.C.F. considered the question of immigration less important than his present motion.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Rubbish.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: He spoke on it.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I spoke on immigration, as a matter of fact.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Let me continue with my remarks, and hon. members may rise in their places and speak for themselves, or, if they wish, contradict what I am saying. But I should like to say this, that if the leader of the C.C.F. had a sister, a daughter or a mother in. a displaced persons camp, he would not have made the motion. It is fine to stand in the House of Commons and criticize the government for the little which the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) and one or two other ministers have done in agreeing to bring in a few of these people to Canada. But the fact remains that the question of displaced persons is one of the most acute questions facing the United States government, the British government, or any other government which has anything to do with this matter.
The leader of the C.C.F., I presume after reading the statement made the other day by Mr. Mosher, and thinking it would be a popular stand to take in the House of Commons-

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, apart from the fact that that is untrue, the hon. member has no right to impute motives to any other member in the house. He is doing that, and I ask that it be withdrawn. That sort of thing is pretty contemptible.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka) must not impute motives to any other member.
Labour Conditions

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I have no intention of imputing motives, but I do presume that the leader of the C.C.F. must have read Mr. Mosher's statement.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: As a matter of fact I have not.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: It was exactly along the lines which the hon. member has adopted.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: As a matter of fact I have not read it.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Did the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) read it as well?

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
If the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has not read it, then it is a strange coincidence.
May I say at once that I am not defending the immediate immigration policy of the present government. I feel it has been at least a year and a half too late in any action it has taken. Therefore I say that I am not defending the government's immediate immigration policy. But I must say this, that if we have individuals within this nation who are willing to undertake to bring in a number of persons whom they can employ, then, I say, such individuals are rendering a great service, both to the displaced persons and to Canada.. And the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Dionne) from the very fact that he has undertaken to bring in about a hundred girls, has done so much for these people that I am certain his name is now known to every person in the displaced persons camps.
As I listened to the ramblings across the floor this afternoon, when hon. members were poking fun at one another while discussing this tragic issue, I concluded it was nothing to be proud of. This is one of the most tragic situations that has ever faced the defenceless and homeless people of Europe. And yet the leader of the C.C.F.-*

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: And the leader of the Social Credit party.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Will the hon. member allow me to speak for myself, please? I know that the C.C.F. group believe in dictating their views to everybody else, but I want to speak for myself. Perhaps it was the intention of the hon. member to throw me off my line of thought. Just the same, I think I can make clear what I have in mind.
If the leader of the C.C.F. were sincere in this issue he would have risen in his place and placed a proposition before the government asking it to pass an order in council to guarantee that these girls will not be underpaid. That would have been a noble stand on his part. He did not do that. Oh, no, he wanted
[The Deputy Speaker.]
to create an issue and raise the bogey of these people coming in, in order to hinder public opinion on the question of immigration. Hon. members who have constituents who have mothers, daughters, sons and other relatives in displaced persons camps have been endeavouring to prod the government ahead a little so that something might be done to protect these people. When the order in council was placed on Hansard we immediately heard the cry from the C.C.F. group. For two or three weeks they have been heckling the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell). At first it looked as though they just wanted to find out from the minister certain information, but the fact remains that they are showing opposition to the relief of these unfortunate displaced persons. That is the stand of that group. For too long has that group been appealing to people of other than Anglo-Saxon origin for support. They have now shown their true colours as to where they stand on this issue.
I travelled through Europe for several months and I found that these people did not have a friend in the world. They have been moved around from place to place. It was admitted in the senate committee on immigration and labour that the directors of displaced persons camps had moved people from camp to camp as many as five times in three months, in order to force them to go back under soviet rule. It is an awful state of affairs when people are moved so often and made so miserable. As soon as they had built up their little churches in the camp, as soon as they had suitable places in which to sleep and study, as soon as they had places in which to teach their children, the order to move would come from headquarters run by gentlemen with the same mentality as those who are sponsoring this motion.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: That is a lie.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I want to thank the hon. gentleman for his kind word. That was the first word that came to his mind and it indicates the range of his vocabulary. These people have been made so miserable for two years that it is time we had a few more Mr. Dionnes. I should like to see hon. members of various groups rise in their places and say that if the Dionne mills exploit these girls they will protest and demand that the government do something to protect their interests. But instead we are having the issue confused so that labour will not want to have these people come in. That is not the right thing to do. These displaced persons have no money, and surely it is a noble thing for some one in Canada to be willing to pay their fares in order to save these people. A certain

Labour Conditions
portion of their pay will be deducted, but that will work no hardship on them and in the meantime their lives will be saved.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
My friends can jibe. If they want to get me warmed up, I will get ready. The best of the displaced persons are being creamed off by the South American countries and others. If we do not hurry we shall not get the best type of people. I am glad that there are industrialists who want to bring in these people. It seems to me that by moving the present motion the C.C.F. group is taking a slap at private enterprise. Perhaps some hon. members did not notice it, because the motion was couched in such a way that they felt it was a good thing to support it. But the facts of the situation are that it is a slap at industry for trying to bring in these people,. As far as I am concerned I want to congratulate industry upon trying to bring in these people.
In the British zone in Germany people are supposed to be fed 1.550 calories a day, that is, members of the adult working population. However, in reality the military authorities and UNRRA have been forced to cut that down to between 1,000 and 1,100 calories a day, which is one-third of the calories required by a working man. Can we let these people starve? Can we let them be faced with slow starvation? Surely we must take them out.-In the United States zone they would like to feed the people 2.000 calories a day, but in reality they are able to give them only from 1,500 to 1.600 calories a day, just one-half of what a normal adult requires to keep healthy.
If anyone agrees to bring in one or 100 or 1,000 of these persons it would be only right to let him do so. I asked the head of the camp at Hanover where I visited, how many children there were in the camp. He told me there were 900. Then I asked about their health and he told me that ninety-three out of the 900 were T.B. cases. I think hon. members will agree that that is a high proportion. Are we to sit back and attack the minister for allowing a few of these people to come in and thus reduced the problem in Europe?
It is in the interests of Great Britain; it is in the interests of the United States; it is in the interests of Canada to reduce the displaced persons problem as quickly as possible. You cannot sign a peace treaty with Austria and leave displaced persons there. You cannot sign a peace treaty with Germany and leave displaced persons there. The pre-war population of the United States zone of Germany, if my memory serves me correctly, was 13,000,000 people, but today, on account of
the number of Germans who have been expelled from the territory held by Poland and Czechoslovakia, there are 18,000,000 people. That area simply cannot support that population.
The food required by some of the displaced persons in the British zone is derived from German sources. Surely we should realize that. I cannot understand how mature men -some of them are at least big enough physically-cannot see through the problem and hope to have this European problem solved. Surely it is about time they studied the situation. Time is running on; this is one of the most acute problems of today, and it must be solved.
A number of my constituents and others whom I know across this country have asked for my assistance in trying to get permission from the government to bring in their children and other relatives. A few months ago I asked the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Glen) for permission for certain people to come to Canada. The thing dragged on for months and months. Today I have three letters on my desk saying I need no longer bother because the three girls who were to be brought into Canada are dead. I could give you their names, Mr. Speaker. This is not something to wrangle and joke over in the house; it is serious.
I sincerely congratulate the Minister of Labour and other ministers who have consulted with him on having agreed to issue permits to bring in some of these displaced persons. The lives of these unfortunates are so miserable that I plead with hon. members and .with all groups in the house not to use this issue cheaply, not just play around with it, because it is too tragic.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had intended to deal particularly with one point on speaking to the motion moved by my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). However, since he took his seat there have occurred in this debate a number of incidents to which I wish to refer before proceeding with what I had intended to say.
May I say this-and I say it with a considerable degree of sadness-that I regret that any member of this house should consider it necessary for him to stoop to the depths of misrepresentation and misinformation that the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka) did.

Coldwell (Rosetown-Biggar):	Mr. Speaker, I am going to join those tonight who have expressed regret that the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen) has not presented something of a policy to the house, when we are discussing the important measure which is before us. speechtext:
If the hon. member for
Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) would listen a little more and keep that other organ shut a little more he might learn something. Apparently the Department of Labour had no way of finding out- what was being done to some of these Polish soldier immigrants, because no action was taken until the case was finally dragged into the courts. Apparently this unfortunate immigrant had nowhere to appeal until things came to such a pass that he could lay a criminal charge. It was only then that the Department of Labour acted. I say that that is not good enough.
I wish to have it distinctly understood that I am just as much in favour of having- as many people from the displaced persons camps in Europe brought into this country as any other hon. member. In fact I consider it a disgrace to this country that we have not thousands of them in at this time. These people should have been brought in and given sanctuary under a proper government plan. I am distinctly opposed to any industrialist or corporation being allowed-or, as it appears now, being the agents of the government- to bring people in to work under contract labour. I contend that we have had experiences enough in the past to be a warning to the government that this en bloc immigration is not desirable when it is brought about by people who can make use of them for their own selfish ends. Especially do I object to that apparently being the government's only policy under which we can help these people in the displaced persons camps. When we find, as I have no doubt other hon. members have-and I would not be surprised if every hon. member has had considerable correspondence from people in his own constituency who are endeavouring to bring people over from the central European countries- people writing us letters about their relatives in Europe we have to stop and think. I have had letters from people in my own constituency who have been endeavouring to bring relatives over from France, Czechoslovakia,

Labour Conditions
Austria, Hungary, Germany and all the other countries of continental Europe. These people have been willing to undertake that they will take care of their relatives in displaced persons camps, but they simply cannot get any action from the immigration branch.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: You cannot get an answer to a letter.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I have in my files hundreds of letters from people in my constituency who have been trying for the past three years and more to get people from the displaced persons camps, but there is no action. I will cite one as an example. This man wrote me a letter and later he came to see me. He had been in correspondence with the immigration branch for months, and after he came to see me I took the matter up with them on his behalf again. This man had a niece who was born in Czechoslovakia. She was the only living person left in the family. The only relative she had was her uncle in this country. All the other members of that family had been killed during the time that the German army overran that part of Czechoslovakia. At the time this girl was between sixteen and seventeen years of age. She wandered from pillar to post and from one part of the country to the other until finally she landed in Sweden. There, either through the Red Cross or UNRRA, I forget which, she was able to establish contact with her uncle who was living in my constituency. As I say, that man had for months and months tried to get action. Since then, more than a year has gone by and there is still no action.
Just the other day I received a letter from a friend of mine who, by the way, was himself an immigrant from England years ago. He wrote on behalf of another person who emigrated to this country from Hungary. Mter a considerable amount of correspondence with the immigration branch, the other day this man received a letter from the Winnipeg office of the immigration branch as follows:
Dear Sir:
I have for acknowledgment your letter of May 7 in connection with your application for the admission to Canada of Mr. and Mrs. John Weiss and Mr. and Mrs. Peter Reiter and family.
Your applications were acceptable at the time they were submitted but the immigration regulations have since been amended and, as your relatives are of enemy alien citizenship, their admission to Canada cannot be authorized at the present time.
At the time their applications were submitted, the immigration branch says that they were acceptable. I want to read a few lines R3166-235
from a letter of the man who wrote me and sent me a copy of the letter I just read. He said:
. . . the fact that these people are a son and grandchildren of a Canadian who came to Canada and was a pioneer of this district, 1906, his homestead was-
He gave the location of it.
-where he lived and died but not before receiving his citizenship papers. Mr. Weiss the applicant for entry of his brother is living on and farming this land today and will turn dwelling and land over to his brother as a home immediately he is allowed to enter Canada. He will as also stated give bonds or any required security guaranteeing these people will not become a public charge in any way.
I contend that when citizens of this country who have proven thmselves to be honest and worthy citizens are trying to obtain permission to have relatives of their own come to Canada and are prepared to go bond for them and cannot obtain that permission but find every turn that they make tangled up with a snarl of red tape and the immigration branch bogged down with a bunch of rulings so that no one seems to know what to do, it is time that we protested. When conditions such as that exist I protest against the fact that the government by order in council can set aside a previous order in council and authorize certain industrialists to bring people in for their own benefit.
This morning I read in the paper that some of these girls were interviewed and are alleged to have said that they looked on Mr. Dionne as a benefactor. I say, Mr. Speaker, that when we go to any length-and I contend that we should go much farther and faster than we have gone in bringing in people from displaced persons camps-to bring people into the country they should look to Canada and to the people of Canada as their benefactors, and not to certain individuals.
In closing, I should like to ask a few questions. I wonder how the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) likes what has been going on. Judging by what he has been saying in connection with this matter, I wonder how he can sit quietly by and see things of this kind going on. I ask all hon. members on the government side to stop and consider whether we have done our duty to displaced persons in the past. If they do that I am satisfied that their answer must be no.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I do not wish, by silence, to give consent to this style of contract. I am not interested in criticizing the government, because the same head-on collisions and conditions of affairs with regard to these industries prevailed after the last great war and have resulted after all the wars. Business has been upset, and we have had industrial destruction and the evils of industrial cut-throat competition and all that kind of thing. I am interested in seeing that the proper safeguards are placed in this labour contract.
In the first place, we had the very same kind of conditions after the last war. Cheap, shoddy Japanese goods were coming into this country. Many goods came in here, notwithstanding the tariff of the United States and the countries in Europe. The result was that an Alien Labour Act was passed in this country by a Conservative administration. Another Conservative administration appointed a committee of the House of Commons, known as the Stevens committee on price spreads and mass buying, the report of which was later adopted and evils adjusted. That committee found that a dreadful state of affairs existed in the textile industry and many of the other industries, and in some of the largest stores. It held many sittings and brought in a report. Safeguards were recommended to parliament. I think some of them were adopted by the present government and some by the late government headed by Mr. Bennett.
How does this particular contract come about? I ask that question simply for information. I sympathize greatly with the government in having to solve these problems which have grown out of the war and for which we in the House of Commons are to some extent responsible. In the first place, we have had the Alien Labour Act placed on the statute books of this country. What for? To protect us in case of peace or of war. to protect our industries and both capital and labour. The responsibilitity for the enforcement of the law is on not only the federal government but the provincial attorneys gen-

Labour Conditions
eral as well. This Alien Labour Act is a federal statute, but as I see the operation of it, the enforcement is on the dominion and on the provinces as well. I do not like the method and manner in which the contract before us for this industry has been proposed and entered into. I have for many years, in peace and war alike, espoused the cause of the Polish nation. I believe I have on many occasions brought to the attention of this house the sufferings of that great nation in the last great war and also in the one which has just closed. I am not objecting to a reasonable number of these refugees being brought into this country, because it is at the request of the British government. The United States has done little or nothing up to date, but I understand that the President-who has had a large number of important matters to deal with-has now consented to take 100,000 refugees into that country.
I wish to point out some of the other features in connection with this contract. First of all, I believe it is improvident from the point of view of the poor girls who are coming out to this country. They will no doubt make good citizens. I have known a great many Polish people in our city and in other places, and I have no criticism at all to make of them. They have always been good citizens and most of them or nearly all have never been in any trouble. I also want to point out to the government that the textile industry-and this contract deals with a particular branch of it in the province of Quebec 

was one of the matters dealt with by the Stevens inquiry. If you are to allow contracts with regard to priorities in shipping, ocean and air, to be made in connection with this particular industry, are you to repeat that for every other industry that wants a cheaper form of labour from Europe and Asia? You will have a large number of these applications. There are some thirty or forty different nationalities, according to the "Canada Year Book," who will want equality of treatment. The same treatment which is given the Polish girls in one industry in the province of Quebec will have to be extended to other races as it is for refugees as to farming and logging. Many of those who come in have no practical experience in these industries. Some have admitted, since they came in, that they have not any experience in farming or in logging. If hon. members will read report No. 6 of the senate committee on evidence given before it re immigration and labour, they will find that what I say is correct. Some admit they were never engaged in farming or logging.
The next point I wish to make is that, in an economic sense, industry in England is in the most awful state it has ever been in at any time in the history of the country since the industrial revolution, the textile industry included. The people of England have lost their foreign investments. They are losing their cotton trade with India. The United States has taken their place. Today much of industry has collapsed and is practically ruined in the old country. Many of those engaged in it are leading skilled people whom we should have had in the textile and other skilled industries in this country. I would point out that some of the heads of Eaton's and Simpson's, some of their departmental managers, and many of the directors of other great industries in this country, have come from Belfast in Ireland, from Scotland, Wales and England and made a success here. I find that some of them later, on promotion, became heads of these great industries and departmental stores in this country. I just mention that to show that, while the proposal is to bring in people from almost every other country on the same basis and grant a contract on different priorities, we are forgetting all about our own people in the old land, in Great Britain, at a time when they are down and out. We forget all about the fact that they could meet the need in many of these industries and do the very work which we want done, as leaders and developers, in the great industrial development which this country should have after the war and in the period of reconversion. Also girls for nursing and as housekeepers and maids are wanted. Are we to allow these people to go to Australia and New Zealand? There they are getting assisted passages to work in textile woollen industries. This form of assisted passage in this Quebec contract is one which I do not like, under which you are going to take out of the pay envelope a certain amount of money for the passage and a certain amount more for clothing, leaving a mere pittance for the individual to live on. You will remember that one of the abuses mentioned in the Stevens report was that under these somewhat cheap labour conditions some people were not able to make enough to pay for their food, and were starving on a pittance of wages. Many of them could not get a loaf of bread in the house under the intolerable conditions which were revealed in that report, and as a result changes had to be made.
I am not here to justify anything that has been done in this member's Quebec contract, and certainly I would not try to justify these
Labour Conditions

contracts. The responsibility is upon the government of the day. If this policy is going to interfere with competitive labour; if it is going to lead to cut-throat competition between this company and other companies throughout Canada who get no similar or adequate protection along these lines, I say the responsibility is upon the government. We have an Alien Labour Act which these other companies must obey. They must conform to dominion labour laws, provincial laws and all the rest of it, and they can get no labour aid from the mother country at all on account of the lack of shipping. I know of two or three industries which have been trying to bring in a few people from the old country, but they cannot get them. The premier of Ontario has just returned and told us there are a hundred thousand in England who would like to come to this country but who cannot get shipping accommodation.
I regret that our very fine minister of immigration has been ill. It is no wonder, with all the hard work he has had to do in connection with this troublesome and other after-war problems. I sympathize with the government in that respect, because the ministers are bearing a heavy burden in connection with these after-war problems. But I do say there should be some equality of treatment in regard to shipping accommodation, and we should bring skilled workers from Britain before it is too late. Many industries in this country would like to have labour of this kind, such as this Quebec company got the government to aid them to bring in, to enable them to undersell their competitors, because this great textile industry is very much diversified today, and was largely expanded as a result of the war. So I plead with the government not to forget about the mother country, which has been a pioneer in this kind of textile work since the industrial revolution, and to aid those skilled in it there, who are out of work, to come here. Many people in Britain would take a chance and come to this country today if they could get accommodation and shipping; but here we are sitting around forgetting all about them; and we see very little in the press and hear very little over the radio about the suffering in that country. They are suffering more than anyone else. Many thousands would like to emigrate to Australia and New Zealand because they believe that to be a white man's country where they would have a fair chance, in the woollen textile and other industries there, to carry on after the great battle they put up in England. Conditions there are far worse than after the battle of Britain. The
working classes are starving at the present time, notwithstanding all that has been said to the contrary. If you do not believe that, just read the British papers; read the white paper that was tabled in the British House of Common, and see the condition of affairs there. The suffering in that country is deplorable.
I should like to see proper safeguards included in the contracts we have been discussing today. I call upon the minister of labour of the province of Quebec as well as our own Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) to take the necessary steps to protect these girls who suffered so much during the war. We in this country were very fortunate; we did not suffer an invasion. It is true that during the first two and a half years of the war we were pretty close to it, and our own province of Quebec and the maritimes and Ontario might have know what it meant to be invaded, but fortunately we escaped. So we should have some regard for those who suffered so much, and I urge that these workers should receive some further contract protection. I believe the contracts are ultra vires under the Alien Labour Act. If it were looked into I believe it would be found that the contracts should have been made with the government, not with any private individual or firm. When a contract is made with a member of parliament it borders on the rights and privileges of members of this house. The member may lose his seat over it, because he cannot make a contract or be party to any contract containing consideration with the government of the day or any department of the government or any commission connected therewith. I believe that is a fair interpretation of the law as it stands; and I think it is going pretty far from that act when an industry has to rely upon influence, because no doubt some influence has been used; you cannot get shipping space without influence. I know; I have tried at some of the shipping companies to bring one or two individuals out here, and I have been told that their space is sold for nearly a year ahead. I believe that in many ways charity should begin at home. I have no doubt that the men and women who have come to Canada from all these other countries have made good citizens; I believe many others would do well here if they had the chance, and I do not oppose a reasonable number being brought in. But I believe the United States should have led the way, and here they are taking only one hundred thousand. We have made a start, but I do believe these girls should have all the protection and safeguards the government of the country can give them.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Acting Minister of Mines and Resources):
maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for

Labour Condilions
the past four days I have been Acting Minister of Mines and Resources, so at the moment I am responsible for the administration of immigration policies of this government. Therefore I think I should say a few words in this debate, even though my background in immigration matters is not extensive.
This afternoon the hon. member for Rose-tovvn-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) moved the adjournment of the house in order to pillory another hon. member who has undertaken to move some displaced persons to this country. I should like to examine the position in the light of the government's immigration policy. In the first place, the government has announced that it is favourable to absorbing into this country our fair proportion of the population of the displaced persons camps in Europe. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has been one of the loudest advocates of that policy. At the united nations he advocated the formation of international committees to move these people from camps in Europe to various countries which are able to absorb them.
The government is favourable to the reception of a very considerable number of immigrants. I believe it is the wish of all parties in the house that an active immigration policy should be pursued, and with that in view the government has been liberalizing the immigration laws of this country for many months past. In January, order in council P.C. 371 was passed which considerably broadened the class of immigrants who could be received in this country. Among the classes to be admitted were "a farm labourer entering Canada to engage in assured farming employment"; "a person engaged in mining, lumbering or logging entering Canada to engage in assured employment in any one of such industries." The assured employment provision has been in all the liberalized regulations, the purpose being to see that immigrants brought here are assured a fair chance to establish themselves in this country. In spite of the liberalized regulations, however, immigrants have not been coming forward. In respect of persons in displaced persons camps, the reason is obvious. These people have no money, and there is no way in which they can get to Canada without assistance. There is no way in which they can conform to the requirements of the act, unless someone will undertake to employ them.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Would the minister permit a question? Does he think it gives the immigrants to this country a fair chance, when they are saddled with a payment over-

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
As I say, in spite of the liberalized regulations, immigrants have not been coming to Canada. The hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Dionne) undertook to put into practice the liberalized immigration policies of the government. He undertook to provide transportation for people who could not themselves provide it. And he undertook to provide assured employment, as is required by the act.
A good deal has been said about the contract for these people. I have not seen the contract, and I think no other member in the house has seen it. And until we know something about it, I think it is premature to discuss the question as to whether or not it is a fair contract.
The hon. member for Beauce spoke to me about transportation. He explained his mission in Europe, and he explained that he was going there to select displaced persons who could reasonably be expected to be happy in the county of Beauce. He explained that it was a Catholic locality and that persons who settled there would be better off if they were members of the Catholic faith. He explained, too, that he had made provision for living accommodation. He had obtained a building which was operated by an order of the Catholic church, where the immigrants would be housed, fed and looked after until they could learn the language of the country. He wanted transportation. I asked him what kind of transportation, and he said he wanted the best transportation. He thought the best kind available was transportation by air. I explained that there were charter companies which could offer various types of accommodation, but he said he wanted the de luxe accommodation, and he suggested that the new aircraft operated by Trans-Canada Air Lines would be the class of accommodation that he wanted for these people. The result was that he made a contract with Trans-Canada Air Lines to send its luxury air liners to pick up these people. I may say that before these prospective immigrants were granted entry, they were screened by the immigration branch, medically examined, and found to be persons who would comply with the immigration laws.
They have now been transported to Beauce, and I think no one in the house would criticize the manner in which they have been treated up to this time. It has been suggested in the house that they are expected over a

Labour Conditions
period of two years to refund the cost of their transportation. I do not know whether that is so or not. I understood, from one statement I read in the press, that they were expected to refund a part of the transportation costs, and that may be so, or they may be expected to refund the full transportation costs.
However it may be, I see nothing extraordinary in that. These people, we must assume, were exceedingly anxious to come to Canada, exceedingly anxious to leave the camps in which they have been living. I have no doubt that they entered into the contract freely, if the contract provided that they should pay back their transportation moneys over a period of time. Whether the contract is enforceable or not, I shall leave to anyone in the house to determine. I presume that, if any one of these girls decides to move away from Beauce, no police officer is going after her to bring her back to serve out the contract. It is simply a civil contract, perhaps calling for the repayment of $300 over two years.
On the other hand, there is another side to the contract. It is that the hon. member for Beauce has undertaken to provide employment for these girls over a period of two years. That contract is enforceable; and, so far as the girls are concerned, I think it is a valuable contract.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Have you seen it?

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: No, and neither have you.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: But you just tell us what the terms are, although a few minutes ago you said you did not know anything about it.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: The reason I am sure of the terms is that the Immigration Act provided in respect of the Polish veterans, and in other comparable cases, that there will be assured maintenance for immigrants for a period of two years. And, knowing that the hon. member for Beauce was required to meet the regulations of the immigration branch, I can say with some certainty that the two-year provision is part of the agreement. I say that with much more certainty than the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) can say that it is not part of the agreement.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Well, the minister knew more than the house does, because no information has been given.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: He knows more than you do.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: You have contributed your five cents worth; will you let me finish?

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I asked a simple question, but the minister does not want to answer it.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: It is more than $300, too.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Well, you succeeded in your purpose, that of throwing me off my line of thought.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: No, I asked a question; that is all.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: You certainly like to play politics over there; you are expert at it.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: The voice of authority.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
In any event, the immigrants brought in by the hon. member for Beauce are now residents of Canada. As such they are entitled to the protection of the laws of Canada. If it is possible to grind down Canadians in employment in industry, then it may be possible to grind down these immigrants. But if it is not-I believe it is not-then I believe Canada has labour laws entirely adequate to maintain the Canadian standard of living. If that is so, the immigrants concerning whom we are now talking will have every protection those laws can afford.
No objection has been made in the house of the immigration of Polish veterans. May I point out that they, too, are under contract, and that the people who are employing them are under contract. That contract provides that the men will be employed for a period of two years, and also provides that they will remain in the employment covered by their contract for a period of two years.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: There are no transportation charges against Polish veterans.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Well why?-because someone paid the transportation charges of these men. In this case it happened to be the British government. Therefore there is no charge accruing.
Other displaced persons will, we hope, be brought to this country. Hon. members of the C.C.F. group probably would be quite happy to do nothing for at least a year, until the international agency charged with the movement of these people is able to function. And I am told that it is a year away. My hon. friend, the leader of the C.C.F., went to Lake Success and advocated that Canada should take displaced persons, and advocated that this international agency be asked to bring these persons to Canada. He is ready to give that great lip service to immigration and to the making happy of all displaced persons. In the meantime, displaced persons are not coming to

Labour Conditions
36S9
this country; they are going to other countries. Why are they going to other countries? They are going to other countries, because citizens of those countries are going to Europe to select immigrants suitable for their countries and are paying the cost of taking them to their countries, doubtless under contract.
It is all very well to advocate great reforms, to advocate that things should be done by some intangible person who does not exist at the moment; it is all very well to say that we are great humanitarians, that we will look after displaced persons if and when some international agency sends them to us, and that everyone should be happy. The hon. member for Beauce happened to be a realist. He believed that displaced persons should be brought to this country and he went over and got them and brought them here and paid for their coming. He has undertaken to look after them for two years. If that is a crime, then he deserves the pillorying that the C.C.F. party is attempting to give him today. But before accepting opposition criticism as valid, I should like to look at the accomplishment. I would rather hear the defence of the hon. member for Beauce of his position when he comes to this House of Commons.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that this is a very simple subject to discuss, but every attempt has been made to confuse it. It has been suggested that we should wait until the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Dionne) is here so that we can discuss the matter with him. We are not concerned with discussing this matter with the hon. member for Beauce; we are concerned with government policy. The Acting Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Howe) has said that the government is liberalizing its immigration policy. I suggest to the government that it stop liberalizing its policy if this is to be the result. This is not liberalizing any policy.
Let us look at the picture. On April 22, on the orders of the day, I asked the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen) a question about a report appearing in the papers of that date, that a member of parliament had gone to Europe to select people for his factory from the displaced persons camps. The minister replied, as reported on page 2279 of Hansard, as follows:
I have not seen the newspaper item to which the hon. gentleman refers, but I would repeat what I said the other day to the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon). So far as any new policy on immigration is concerned, it will be announced in due course.
That was on April 22. But in a return issued at the request of the hon. member for
Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), being sessional paper 678, among other items I find this:
Certified to be a true copy of a minute of a meeting of the committee of the privy council, approved by His Excellency the Governor General on the 1st April, 1947.
On April 1, three weeks before I had asked my question, the government by this order in council had set aside its former policy on immigration as authorized by P. C. 695 since 1931 and had adopted a new policy to permit the hon. member for Beauce to bring in 100 persons from displaced persons camps in Europe to work in his factory.
The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka) painted a very good picture of the desperate condition of those in the displaced persons camps. We are all agreed that their position is desperate, but let me tell the house that their desperation was not the reason why they were brought to Canada. I should like to quote from a letter written by the hon. member for Beauce to the deputy minister of labour under date of November 26, 1946, in which he said:
I know that this permission can be given to me if you care to talk the matter with the minister, and I would like you to do so. I know Mr. Mitchell and I am positive he will do everything he can to help me.
Not to help persons in the displaced persons camps, but to help the hon. member for Beauce.
I hope that you will reconsider this situation in the light of emergency on which I am placed and will act accordingly.
That was not an emergency facing the persons in the displaced persons camps; the emergency was the position in which the hon. member for Beauce was placed through not being able to get people for his mills. It has been suggested that these people would be glad to get away from the displaced persons camps. There is no doubt in the world of that, but it is equally evident that the girls who worked in the Beauce mill were also anxious to get away, because 555 out of a total staff of 425 got away from there in one year.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Seasonal work.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: It is time that we stopped talking about this thing having been done on the basis of humanity. It was not done on the basis of humanity; it was done on the basis of pure, cold, business.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: The C.C.F. should talk about bringing in immigrants.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
We are quite pleased to have immigrants brought in, but we will not,
Labour Conditions

without protest, allow them to be brought in by industrialists going over to the displaced persons camps in Europe where these people have been congregated, where they are anxious to get away from their misery and distress, and feeling their arms and muscles, examining them to see if they are fit to work. I should like to quote from another letter by the hon. member for Beauce. This letter is addressed to the Minister of Mines and Resources under date of March 26, 1947, and he says:
As I am going across myself, I will visit these girls personally so that I can make sure that they are fit for the work that they will have to perform in my mill.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Of course that is right. I am saying that is the reason they were brought here and I say that is wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: You want to leave them there.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
My hon. friend was
brought up in the cradle of Liberalism, but it seems to me that he must have fallen out of it early in life when he is willing to approve conduct like that.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Do you want them to remain where they are?

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I do not want to leave them where they are, but I do not want anyone to exploit their misery.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: What are you exploiting now?

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Nothing, and my hon. friend knows it.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I know no such thing. It is the contrary, I should think.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: These people are refugees. A refugee is a person who is seeking sanctuary. When you provide refuge for a person seeking sanctuary you do not consider how much gain you can get out of it. You consider what help you can give to that refugee.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: The main thing is to give him sanctuary. You would keep him in slavery.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: These girls have actually gone into slavery now.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: You should be ashamed of yourself.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: The turn-over in this plant of 425 employees in a year is great. There were 555 taken in and left in a year.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I know the hon. member wants to be fair-

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Of course I want to be fair, but you people don't.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Don't accuse me of that. Will my hon. friend not admit this that in the small town industries there is a great deal of seasonal employment.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
What is seasonal
employment?

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I know what I am talking about. My hon. friend does not. There is a greater turn-over by the very nature of things in the small town industries of Ontario and Quebec than in other provinces where they have not the same amount of seasonal labour.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I have read the whole of the file, and nowhere has the hon. member for Beauce said that this was a seasonal industry. If it is a seasonal industry, how is he to guarantee employment to these girls for two years if he could not guarantee employment for two years to the citizens of Quebec?

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Regardless of how he can, he is guaranteeing it, and the immigration branch will hold him to his contract.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I do not know whether he is or is not, and I do not think the minister knows, because he said a few minutes ago that he did not.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I did not say that. I said I had not seen the contract.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
My understanding is that the contract was not made with the government of Canada or with anybody in Canada, but with the officials of UNRRA. I have here the Montreal Standard of May 31, containing an interview with Mr. James Adams, general manager of the plant. This is what Mr. Adams says:
This business of the two-year contract, that wasn't Mr. Dionne's idea at all. The allied commission insisted upon it. He is responsible for the welfare of the girls for the next two years.
So this government does not know anything about it, and it is not on the record that the government ever demanded a contract. It goes on:
After that, if they want to go somewhere else, they can. But their contract is for two years.
Outside of that, no minister on the other side of the house can say with any assurance that there is anything in writing that will protect the interests of these girls.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
There is the law of the land.	.
