maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: There is very little law of the land in the province of Quebec so far as the workers are concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: That is not correct.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
That is the fact. What we object to is not the bringing in of these people. We have asked that the government of Canada bring these people into Canada as free people, giving them a chance to make their own way and go their own way whenever they want to. We will not allow people with commercial interests to serve to go into these camps, pick out whom they want and leave those they do not want, and then say they are performing a public service. It is nothing of the kind. It is pure, straight commercialism, and it is something this government should be definitely ashamed of.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
As one who has been interested in the question of immigration and the plight of displaced persons and refugees, and who has had something to say about it from time to time, I wish to say a few words on this occasion; my main purpose being to point out what, in my opinion, is the shortcoming of the present policy of the government, and second, to clear up some of the charges and misunderstandings that have been created in the house this afternoon. Before doing that, I wish to remind the house that we are discussing the motion moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), leader of this group, and to read a line or two from the motion to set out its purpose. These words will, I think, set out what we are trying to impress upon the government and the house:
The selection of displaced persons and refugees and their admission to this country should be directed entirely by the federal government with a view to resettling these people as free human beings in such a way as to serve their best interests and those of the Canadian people as well.
That is the object of bringing before the house this motion which started this discussion. I wanted to place that on record, because some of the charges and some of the statements that have been made this afternoon have beclouded the issue. It was not our purpose to make any political capital out of the situation.

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: No, never!

maintopic: DISPLACED PERSONS BROUGHT TO CANADA BY INDUSTRIALISTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
And we have not
attempted to do so.
If there is something to be made, why not make it?
That is frank.
It means something, too.

But if other members ' insist on having it on a political basis, then, of course we have nothing to hide and are quite willing to put our position before the house. However I have never personally felt that this is a question which should be placed on a political basis, certainly not on a partisan basis, because it is a question which affects all parties in the house and all the people of the country. I do not think anything can be gained by making charges which cannot be supported or by making statements which are contrary to the facts. My criticism of the government is with regard to the policy which is now being followed; and I gather from the speech of the Acting Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Howe) today that that is the present government policy; in other words, that it is not an isolated incident, but is a step along the line of government policy. If that is so, I wish to say, in all earnestness and without any acrimony whatsoever, that it is not the best way to go about the matter.
For example, as the government and the acting minister know full well, there have been thousands of applications waiting, some for two years and some for longer, by people in Canada who have relatives in displaced camps in Europe, people here in Canada who, on their own initiative, are willing to take the responsibility of bringing these people to this country, paying their passage if necessary, and guaranteeing employment and a home for them here. The relatives in Canada of displaced persons in camps in Europe are anxious to bring these people here, not because they want to exploit them. Let it be clear that they want to bring them here because they feel, having had the privilege of entering this country themselves and being now in a position to help their compatriots who are not in as good a situation, that they are willing to sacrifice something of what little wealth they have in order to help their brethren. It is in that spirit that the applications were made and submitted to the government. I have had some personal experience, as other hon. members have had, and know something about what is going on behind these applications. I can say, without any fear of contradiction, that ninety-five per cent or more of these applications were made from a purely humanitarian point of view, trying to help somebody out. Under these circumstances it would appear that the government should be prepared to cooperate

Labour Conditions

in the same spirit by putting the whole question on a humanitarian basis; that is, by allowing refugees and displaced persons to come to this country to find sanctuary, not because of what they can add to the immediate wealth of the country, but because they are in great need. In some cases, if their health is impaired, they might even be a liability to the country for a little time, but that should not deter us from assisting them.
As I said, these applications have been lying by the thousands in the hands of the immigration branch and very little has been done about the matter. The results have been disappointing. I think everybody will admit that. At the moment I am not criticizing anyone in particular when I say that. The government have had reason, perhaps, why they were not able to expedite the disposal of these applications as they should have done. But while that is going on, while thousands of people in this country who have relatives in Europe and who have submitted applications and made every guarantee that was asked of them to the government and were waiting for action, they find that other persons who are not doing it on the same basis-let us be frank about that; it is not done on a basis of bringing in relatives for humanitarian purposes; it is done to bring in labour for certain industries-are getting priority so far as transportation and permission are concerned. Special orders in council have been passed to give these people priority over those who are attempting to bring in their relatives. That is the basis of my criticism.

May I ask the hon. member
a question? What is the priority that has been given?

It is quite clear from
the order in council which was quoted today, which set aside the provisions of the general order, 695, and gave this particular person the privilege of bringing in a certain group of immigrants while others under the general immigration order have to wait.

The T.C.A. service is open
to all. Anybody can buy seats on the T.C.A.

I do not want to get
into an argument with the acting minister about this. It so happens that not many relatives of displaced persons in Canada are in a position to hire T.C.A. planes to bring their relatives here. I think that is one good reason why they have not done so.
And they would not think of charging it back.

Mr. Speaker, I now for the
first time have the contract in my hand, [DOT]and I refer to clause (d), which reads:
No deduction from the wages will be made by the company for the cost of transportation of the worker from Germany to destination in Canada.

That is not what they
said.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: But that is what the contract says.

Mr. Speaker, I hope
before I am through saying what I have to say, we shall be able to get on the record other facts with regard to the contract.

I rise to a point of
order, Mr. Speaker. The minister has read from a document, and I am asking that the document be tabled.

Certainly. I was waiting for
the opportunity to table a copy of the document.

Why was it not tabled
earlier?
I received it just this minute. It comes from overseas.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member has a suspicious mind; that is all.
We asked for it.

Hon. members over there
have a good sense of publicity.

I said a moment ago,
Mr. Speaker, that those who would like permission to bring relatives to Canada should have been given consideration. The report made last year by the senate committee on immigration and labour bears out that contention. I wish to quote from page 311 of the report submitted by that committee, at which there will be found these words:
Immigrants who come to Canada on the responsibility of relatives or friends already here enjoy a real advantage over those who arrive as complete strangers. The right to bring relatives and friends here is a privilege which our government may well extend to Canadian citizens. This principle has already been recognized by the government in an order in council dated May 28, 1946, P.C. 2071.
But unfortunately, although that principle was admitted by the passage of that order in council, we find that it is only too easy to pass another order in council setting aside the provisions of the former one in order to make special conditions or to apply special privileges to some persons. I wanted to say that, because I believe that the present action of the government, whether it is deliberately

Labour Conditions
taken or not. is short-circuiting our immigration policy. It is not carrying out the intent of parliament.
When my hon. friend talks about short-circuiting, would he say-
Not a speech; just a question.
Just wait a minute. You asked me enough questions this afternoon.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: But we did not get any answers.

Not to my disadvantage. But when my hon. friend talks about short-circuiting, -would he say that bringing to Canada people who are in these camps is short-circuiting the regulations? I know what my hon. friend is trying to do. He is trying to play both ends against the middle.
I want to assure the minister that I am not playing the two ends against the middle. What I am trying to do is to point out that by making these special provisions for privileged persons-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Privileged?
-the government is providing a safety valve for not having to do anything about the general question of displaced persons.
The hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Dionne) is privileged.

I hope that is clear enough. There are, as I said, thousands of those, within the knowledge of the immigration branch. It is not a matter of bringing in one, two or three hundred; it runs into thousands. And the people of this country are, I think, entitled to expect action on the part of the government on that point, because all parties in this house have agreed. Surely that is all that is necessary in parliament. If all parties are agreed on a principle, the government should take action. All parties are agreed that the question of displaced persons and refugees should get some priority. In fact, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself, in making a statement in the house not so long ago, made the statement that displaced persons and refugees would get priority, and the senate committee recognized that, as I just quoted a minute or two ago. I do not know whether the minister was in his seat at the time.

Order. May I call the attention of hon. members to a matter of procedure and ask them to confine their remarks to the motion before the house. This afternoon the leader of the C.C.F. party asked 83166-236J
for leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 31. Standing order 31 says:
Leave to make a motion for the adjournment of the house (when made for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance) -

For a great many years that had become both the written policy and the practical application of the policy by the officers of the department. One of the first things done after our return from the meeting of the assembly of the united nations was to provide an amendment to P.C. 695 to authorize persons resident in Canada to bring in persons related to them who happened to be in displaced persons camps. That amendment was adopted on January 30, 1947.
That did not have any immediate result. Although the obstacle which theretofore had existed as a legal obstacle was removed, there were still many physical obstacles that had to be overcome. It was necessary for these

I have not seen it; I am told that it is well fitted out, quite a comfortable building, well provided and equipped for the residence of these girls, but it is under the direction of some nuns. He said, "None but Catholic girls would be at all happy in these surroundings." I think that is true. I do not know how happy the Catholic girls are. From the pictures that have been published in the papers they were at least happy on arrival. I hope that that joy will continue. But that is the situation, and I was impressed by the fact that these girls were to get the same kind of treatment that a member of parliament provides in his own constituency for the daughters of his own constituents. It seemed to me that that would be nothing very deplorable and that, in any event, it would be fortunate for these persons to get from these displaced persons camps to the kind of hostel under the conduct of a religious community of Catholic nuns, which is operated in the town of St. Georges.
There is this other group that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar referred to as being something with respect to which he was quite in accord, a group that would be brought out because not only the employer but the representatives of trade unions would assist in the selection or in the making of arrangements That may be all right. I do

Labour Conditions
not see that the presence of representatives of labour unions will make the situation very much better.
The whole problem is this. Is it a bad thing that there should be an additional number of people willing to work coming into this country? That is the question. If they are willing to work in the kind of jobs for which enough workers are not available I think they will be improving their own position, and I am not at all scandalized if they also at the same time improve the economic situation of the country. I think that if all the displaced persons in these camps could get into places where they would be contributing to the economy of the lands to which they will go they will be far happier if they are brought into lands where they are not a charge upon the rest of the community.
I know it is often said that one did not intend to participate in the debate-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member cannot say that.

I can. I have listened all afternoon to the arguments advanced, the argument of the affable Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) when on behalf of the government he raised the defence that the house should wait until the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Dionne) was in the house to explain the situation to the country. That argument was not effective because, Mr. Speaker, so far as the hon. member for Beauce is concerned he enters into this question only to the extent that he happens to be the employer. The responsibility-and the minister who has just taken his seat has admitted it-does not rest on the hon. member for Beauce. The responsibility for what took place, if there be such, rests upon the government and not upon the hon member. To that extent, at least, some of the underbrush during the course of the debate has been cleared away.
Matters have been brought in which have aroused animosities and antipathies and which have no place in this debate. The question, sir, is that the house be adjourned to discuss the question as to whether the traditional policy of parliament that the importation of indentured labour should be completely prohibited, shall be departed from. Do we in Canada want to establish an immigration policy by which employers in our country will be able to go over to Europe, there select displaced persons and make arrangements with them to pay their transportation out of the wages they will ultimately earn-
No, no.
-and then bring them over to Canada? That is the question.
No, no.

My hon. friends say it is not, and to prove that statement I shall read from the records. The government agreed to just that. The government entered into an arrangement with the hon. member for Beauce in consequence of a lengthy correspondence. I am not going to read very much of the record, but I am going to read from the correspondence that is before the house one or two bits which indicate what the plan was. There is first the letter to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), in which the policy and the reasons for it are outlined. The reason for asking for a departure from the ordinary immigration laws in effect in this country- and I quote from the letter-was as follows:
The trouble seems that the people have too much money to spend. They work for three or four months and then they go away and live on unemployment funds for a while and go to some other place when they are through with unemployment help.
The purpose behind the application was to assure that when these people came to Canada they would not be free to leave at the end of three or four months but would continue as employees for the period for which they were indentured, namely, a period of two years.
My right hon. friend has dealt with the humanitarian side. No party has any monopoly on that. All of us believe that displaced persons, those who suffered as none of us may ever dare to understand, however one tries, should receive assistance. These unfortunate persons want to get out of camps and go to various parts of the world. Other parts of the world are welcoming them. Canada has been notoriously deficient in performance of what we should have endeavoured to achieve in this regard. We know what our Polish allies did during the period of the war. The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka) spoke with understandable feeling. We know what our Ukrainian allies did. In the province of Saskatchewan family after family have relatives of those two racial origins whose contribution has been great in this country as has been that of those left behind in the old land. They are fine citizens. The question is: shall we in this parliament approve a makeshift system designed apparently to meet the needs of one employer in this country? Other employers are in a different position. The Minister of Labour said today that this order
Labour Conditions

in council of April 1 is the only one of its kind. There may have been one or two subsequently-
Not of that nature.

Not of that nature, we are told. So what we are asked to approve is an order in council passed on April 1 and what has taken place thereunder. How was that order in council passed? What policy did the government follow? Is it a policy of welcoming to our country, by selective immigration, men and women who would make good citizens? No. It may be only the thin end of the wedge, but it is a policy that will either be continued or discontinued, and we have not any assurance with regard to that point. Upon what is the policy based? Here are the terms of the agreement as contained in a letter of March 26, 1947, from the hon. member for Beauce addressed to the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen): That letter reads as follows:
Pursuant our conversation of this afternoon, I respectfully ask you to give me a permit to import 100 foreign girls or widows to work in my spinning plant "Dionne Spinning Mills Co." at St. George, Beauce.
These girls will take their headquarters at the convent-
Then it sets out the exceptionally fine circumstances under which they will live.
Read all the letter.

Very well.
-which is situated five hundred feet from the mill and is under the direction of the Sisters of the Good Shepherd.
And with that there will be no argument. To continue:
I will pay the transportation of these girls from their homes to Canada. I will see that these girls or widows are healthy morally and physically. I will comply with the rules and regulations of the Canadian government.
The next paragraph is the significant one. It reads:
I will make a contract with these girls to refund me their transportation charges at about 25 per cent of what they will earn weekly in my plant. I will' pay these girls, when they begin x>
work, according to the ordinance No. 5 regu-ating the salaries and conditions of work of tex-;ile industries in the province of Quebec.
May I point out at this point, "I will make a contract" and "25 per cent of what they will earn w'eekly" will be deducted. The girls say they made that contract. In the last few days they have given to the press interviews in which they said that they made the contract that the hon. member for Beauce had in mind when he notified the government of his plan on March 26, 1947. The letter continues:

As I am going across myself, I will visit these girls personally so that I can make sure that they are fit for the work that they will have to perform in my mill.
I expect to bring these girls and widows by aeroplane because I understand that the shipping boat facilities are not available presently.
If there is any other regulation that you would like me to comply with I will be glad to do so.
Hoping you will give this matter preferred attention, believe me,
Yours truly,
That is the offer following correspondence over a period of approximately five months. The acceptance is in a letter from Mr. Jolliffe, dated March 27, 1947, which reads as follows:
I would refer to your letters addressed to the minister relative to the admission of young women from Europe for employment by your company. The minister has had two interview's with Mr. Dionne, M.P., and has agreed to the admission of 100 young women. Particulars of the requirements have been given to Mr. Dionne, who will no doubt be communicating with you in due course.
The letter is directed to James A. Adams, Dionne Spinning Mills Company, St. Georges, Beauce, province of Quebec. The order in council, which from its date I take it was based upon the letter, is dated April 1, 1947, and reads:
The committee of the privy council have had before them a report dated March 27, 1947, from the Minister of Mines and Resources, representing that the Dionne Spinning Mill Company of St. George, Beauce, Quebec, have applied tor the admission . . .
And so on. That order in council has already been read into the record. It concludes with these words:
The committee, therefore, on the recommendation of the Minister of Mines and Resources advise that as there is a shortage of textile workers in Canada, the provisions of order in council P.C. 695 dated the 21st March, 1931, as amended, be waived in behalf of 106 immigrants as herein described.
What does this all add up to? It means that the government consented to and approved a policy under which these girls would be brought to this country and twenty-five per cent of the amount they might earn each week would be deducted from their pay envelopes. It never lies within the right of anyone, when later he is asked to face what he has done, to say, that while he agreed to one course, later on he agreed with someone else not to do so. I point out, sir, that the order in council was passed on April 1. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) asked about this matter on April 23 and got no information. Nothing was said about the order in council; not a word. It was just another of those orders in council that get passed and are sometimes forgotten

by the members of the government. They must have forgotten, because on April 23 they did not know anything about it. Parliament was in session, but the order in council in regard to a matter of immigration was forgotten and no information was furnished with regard to it; nor in all the discussions concerning immigration was it. referred to, until after the matter had been brought to the notice of the country through the press. Why? The members of the government who have spoken have not explained the strange situation, in that the government forgot to tell parliament about the order in council and forgot to table the order in council until all arrangements had been completed and concluded. This afternoon production of the contract was asked for by various hon. members. The so-called contract is dated April 14, 1947. It was not in the record. It was not available It came to light only tonight. Whence it came, nobody knows. All we know is that today, just before the dinner recess, the ministers denied that they had it, and tonight it appears. And how the government grab hold of that so-called contract! The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply said transportation charges were not going to be deducted, according to the contract. But that is not what the contract says.
Oh, oh.

I would like anyone in this country to try to enforce a contract between A and B, with A saying, "I had this contract with B but C, who had nothing to do with it, made a different arrangement with me." That is the situation.
Oh, oh.

Let me read a portion of the letter of April 14 to the secretary of the intergovernmental committee on refugees, 19 Hill street, London, which says:
No deduction from the wages will be made by the company for the cost of transportation of the worker from Germany to destination in Canada.
(Signed) Dionne
How is that enforceable in Canada by the girls, who were not party to it and who came to Canada under a different arrangement made between the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Dionne) and the government of this country? My hon. friends found at last a straw upon which to lean, but when it is looked into
Complete drivel.

My right hon. friend is more qualified than anyone in this house to speak about quibbles.

Labour Conditions	____
Because I have listened to so much of it.

He has listened to so much; but we have never been able to change him during a current session. We have often changed him in a subsequent session, when he has had opportunity to think the matter over and realize that we were right. I say, sir, that this was just an out for the government. They did not know it existed until late this afternoon. They did not act upon the so-called contract of April 14. Their contract and the agreement they acted upon was the arrangement they made on March 27, ratified as it was by the order in council. I am not going into further details, but when a contract has been made between certain parties I ask, is it possible to change it subsequently as between one of the original parties and a third party? The only way a government can make an arrangement is by order in council or formal agreement. In this case they made it by order in council; and the explanation given this evening is a mere exculpation found after the event. If the debate this afternoon has succeeded in convincing the government that this question of immigration should be faced in this country as a serious problem-

And in the open.
Mr. DIEFENBAKER-yes, brought into the open so that we may know what is going on, and not be hidden behind the doors of a council chamber or yet under a secret order in council, it will have been time well spent.
Oh, oh.

My right hon. friend ridicules that, but, after all, parliament has the right to know what is going on, though he has never believed in that doctrine. During the war the government used to hide behind the cloak that it was not in the public interest. Those days are past. It is now in the public interest that each of us should know what is going on in the immigration branch and what is to be done. We had a lengthy debate on immigration but learned nothing about this. The contract, ratified by the order in council, I say to you, Mr. Speaker, denies the principles of the united nations. We talk about fundamental freedoms and human rights. The first human right mentioned among the many forms of human rights in the several submissions were placed before the committee of the united nations was that nowhere in the world, directly or indirectly should there be established contracts of servitude or voluntary slavery.
While these girls have secured their freedom from the awfulness of the camp, they
Labour Conditions

tome to Canada with their freedom two years delayed, a freedom they must buy with the sweat of their brows. I say, sir, that is not immigration; that is no immigration policy; that is no substitute for an immigration policy.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members will agree that there is in Canada great sympathy for the suffering and displaced persons of Europe. There is a universal desire to help these people. I was pleased today that the plea of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) gained the support of members of the Progressive Conservative party, and the leader of the Social Credit group; but I was sorry that the spirit and objective of the debate was more or less violated by the introduction of a political issue.
Through its inaction I believe the government has permitted a bad situation to develop, a situation which is creating a bad odour in Canada. The whole press is airing it, much to our discredit, and no doubt it is being aired in the United States and throughout the world. I do not think it improves our standing in the united nations to have appearing in our daily papers reports which sound like descriptions of scenes from "Uncle Tom's Cabin", which remind one of the old slave markets where girls were put up at auction with someone looking at their muscles and someone else looking at their teeth.
The result is most humiliating, and the whole problem is not being met, because it is a problem of taking care of several things, namely the need for labour in Canada and for a policy of immigration, and the further need of doing something for the displaced persons who require refuge. We are going back, instead of ahead. We are not being creditably represented by our actions-and I think we have brought this on ourselves.
However I believe the government is grateful to the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Dionne) for doing something about a situation which the government itself has failed to meet. Now the government is taking credit for its high humanitarian ideals in receiving these people. I do not believe it has any right to do that. Personally if I must choose between letting the hon. member for Beauce do something and no one doing anything, I would say, "Let Dionne do it." But I do not think that is a choice we should have to make. The choice is between Canada's facing up to her responsibilities, and letting someone else face up to them. Personally, 
I am glad someone is doing something, but I do not think the right people are doing it or that it is being done in the proper way.
The government should not now be sensitive about criticism, after all these months have passed and no one has done anything in particular. I have on my desk Hansard for 1945, and I open this volume at the proceedings of November 20 of that year where I raised the question with respect to bringing children from Europe. I asked this question of the then minister of national health and welfare:
I should like to address a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I am sorry that I did not have a chance to give him notice of this question. In view of the appalling conditions prevailing in Europe, and the certainty of death from starvation facing millions of children there, what steps are being taken to give refuge to the children of the stricken countries and bring them to this country?
And the then minister said:
I do not know that the question properly falls within the scope of the Ministry of National Health and Welfare.
Then I persisted and asked the question of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), who replied at some length, telling me that there was no transportation, that we had to bring men home from overseas and that that was not the time to think about saving children in Europe.
That was on November 20, 1945. I have another reference, so that my skirts are clear, so far as this thing goes; and so far as I was concerned it was not a political issue. And I, personally, have undertaken the responsibility of keeping ten children alive in Europe, myself, this year.
I believe that we do have a responsibility, and that there are a number of things concerning which all are agreed:
1.	We are agreed as to the misery;
2.	We are agreed as to our responsibility;
3.	We are agreed that Canada can take people; and the fact that one person has been able to take 100 indicates the truth of that assumption, and
4.	I believe we are agreed that there is need for immediate action, because every member has evidence that people who once had filed application forms are now dead. That is because we have not moved quickly enough.
I am sure every hon. member has in his desk files of letters from people in his constituency who wish to bring in cousins, nephews, nieces or in-laws, but who have not

Labour Conditions
been permitted to do so because of the regulations of the government. While those regulations were improved, they were not implemented with proper machinery for screening people out of these depressed areas.
It was left to the hon. member for Beauce to find the machinery, and I think he deserves a lot of credit for being able to do something the government would not do. I, personally, am glad that 100 people are coming; but I think there should be a thousand.
And hon. MEMBER: Thousands.

It should be the government that is bringing them, not one industrialist. Personally, I am glad that the nuns have taken care to look after them, for God knows there is not enough housing in this country for Canadians, themselves. People who have been here for many years cannot get housing. There are families living in chicken coops, families living in improvised garages, and there are thousands of families doubled up with their in-laws, and tearing their hair every day. And then we wonder why we have broken homes! We are short of housing, and I do not know what these girls would do if someone did not do something about housing them. I, for one, have no objection to anyone taking these people in who will take them. But I want to remind the house that we had thousands of families asking to bring relatives into their homes and to assimilate them in their communities, but the government did not find the means or the machinery to enable those people to come. We could have had them today, if we had taken the necessary action.
There are some aspects of the matter which have not yet been considered. Not only must we justify our action, but we must justify our motives and our methods. I believe that our whole development in law has to do with method, and that parliament itself is a monument to method in conjunction with a certain thing we call procedure, based upon justice.
I believe that we have an excellent example of our development in law in the Nuremberg trials. Not only were we interested in justice; we established the most elaborate machinery to carry out the method to see that the ends of justice were served. It is not that we object to people coming into this country- I resent those who get up and say that the C.C.F. is making a political issue of this when they are simply covering up their own failures-we welcome people coming into this country; we have urged for two years now that we bring people in, give them refuge and assistance. But we do say that we must use methods which are compatible with our
British traditions of justice, and we must not violate those things which we have built up over the decades and centuries. That is what we object to.
We say that we have not met the problem by letting the hon. member for Beauce do what we should have done ourselves. I am not so much interested in whether that hon. member is paying the passage of these girls. I think it is pretty well established, after we have read the evidence leading up to the contract and the contract itself-this may not be clear but we suspect it-that the difference between the minimum wage and the lump sum will somehow be worked out to consider the passage money. The correspondence is misleading and not reassuring.
If the hon. member for Beauce is paying the passage, then we are at fault. In the case of the Polish soldiers we let somebody else pay the passage. We let the impoverished British government pay the passage of those soldiers and now we are letting the hon. member for Beauce do it. We are sitting back and refusing to do our share to help the displaced persons of Europe find a home. That is the crux of the situation. We still have not met our obligations, and the government must see to it that the machinery which was made available to the hon. member for Beauce to examine these people in regard to their health is extended so that more people can come in more quickly.
I hope that we will canvass the people who need labour because I am sure there are many having labour difficulties. In some industries there is a shortage of labour. I am sure there are many homes which would take these people. I have a file of letters I received when I went on the air last year during the time placed at the disposal of hon. members to speak to their constituents. At that time I made a plea for the displaced children of Europe. I asked my listeners to write to me and tell me whether they would take a child into their homes and raise it as their own child. I had letters by the dozen, not only from German people wanting German children and from French people wanting French children, but from Scotch people wanting Polish children. Some people wrote in and said that they thought Poland had suffered the most of all and they wanted to help those who had lost more than others. We could have placed thousands of children if we had the machinery to allow the gratitude and sympathy of the people of Canada to flow to Europe and to bring back people who needed help and refuge.
Labour Conditions

Not only have we a responsibility to the people who are strong and most able-if we take only those who can work in our factories and our mills we still have not met our obligations as a Christian nation-but we have also obligations to the people who are broken and ill and we should accept our share of that part of the displaced persons camps. We should not take only those who are able to work in our factories. Having certain industrialists go over to screen off the healthy people and bring them back here is not meeting the situation.
I urge the government not to try to make this-fi political issue. One thing I am getting awfully tired of in Canada is the practice that began to get popular after the last war. Every time anyone complained about rising prices, every time anyone raised the question of employment or old age pensions he was called a communist. It was thought that by washing him out you could wash out his objections. That is a petty, silly and childish move, but a few people still swallow it and a few people are still willing to use it. I hope that the government will not attempt it. I hope that members of other parties will not use it, because it is a pretty thin and weak argument.
We have a moral responsibility that we should meet. We should not leave this matter to the hon. member for Beauce; we should not leave it to private individuals or industrial concerns. Canada as a nation has the responsibility of bringing the people who need homes into touch with the people who want labour. Canada should provide the transportation, the medical facilities for examination and, through the immigration branch establish citizenship rights for these people whom we hope some day will be grateful not to the hon. member for Beauce, but to Canada as a great Christian nation because she has met her obligations.

What is the present method used by the Department of National Revenue in calculating a farmer's total income tax for the years 19411946 in the event of the farmer not previously having filed a return?
Mr. CHEVR1ER:
If the farmer has kept full financial records of his operations, the income tax assessments are based on such data.
Where the farmer has kept inadequate or negligible records it is necessary to reconstruct his income by examination of the growth in the surplus of his assets over liabilities, by analyses of such data as to income as can be secured from reliable sources and from such partial records as to income and expenditure as he has actually maintained. There is no one method of doing this which can be applied uniformly in -all cases, but the procedures conform as closely as possible to recognized accounting principles.

speechtext:
Why is a passport a confidential document?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Mr. Speaker, the answer would, of course, be that a passport is not a confidential document. The application for a passport contains statements which are made by the applicant to the department in order to obtain the passport, and it is considered, unless there are special reasons for publicizing such information, that it should be treated as confidential. Likewise the fact that an applicant has requested or obtained a passport is generally regarded as a matter to which publicity should not be given under ordinary circumstances. The document itself is, of course, not of a confidential nature and the holder is free to disclose its contents to any person.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLYMER CORPORATION OPERATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. In view of statements in the press today to the effect that the drop in the price of crude rubber may affect operations at the Polymer Corporation, is the minister prepared to make a statement to the house at this time? I learned about this just before three o'clock.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLYMER CORPORATION OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I have seen only one press report of the kind referred to and that was in the London, Ontario, Free Press, reading as follows:
Ottawa, June 1. Despite a break in the price of crude rubber, reflecting a rebound in production, operations at Polymer Corporation at Sarnia, a crown-owned synthetic rubber plant, will be unaffected.
During the past ten days or so, prices on far eastern natural rubber have slipped sharply, and this gave rise to reports that the great Sarnia industry would be closed down.
Today an official government source said flatly that any such stories were untrue.
Admittedly the decline in the price of crude had affected that of the synthetic product, but, said the official spokesman, Polymer still could face competition from natural rubber.
The break in crude had been expected this year, but it had not been anticipated that it would come quite so soon. Unless cut-throat price tactics developed, there was little to fear in the market trend, it was stated.
The Polymer concern is operated in the manner of a private company, but comes under the jurisdiction of Right Hon. C. D. Howe, Minister of Reconstruction. This coming week directors of Polymer are expected to confer with the minister. Doubtless the market trend will be discussed, but the Free Press was assured that the meeting was to be "entirely routine."
I did not prepare this press report, but I would consider it wholly accurate.

maintopic: PENITENTIARY ACT
PENITENTIARY ACT

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, May 26, consideration of I he motion of Right Hon. Mr. Ilsley for the second reading of Bill No. 177, to amend the Penitentiary Act, 1939.

maintopic: PENITENTIARY ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when consideration of this measure was adjourned on the 26th of May I had just commenced to speak on penitentiary reform.
I was dealing first with a few suggestions in connection with penitentiary reform, and my first was that the system now in effect requiring regular reports to be made each month should be discontinued in so far as it requires reports to be made almost indefinitely. Some restriction should be placed on reporting, limiting it to a period of, say one year, and so far as those who have served in the armed forces are concerned the requirement in that direction should be removed.
Again, when we discharge men from the penitentiaries they go out equipped with a suit-

maintopic: PENITENTIARY ACT
speechtext:
A suit which everyone
recognizes.

maintopic: PENITENTIARY ACT
speechtext:
A suit which everyone recognizes, as the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox (Mr. Tustin) points out, and a pair of shoes which can be identified by all. The result is that the man goes out into civilian life ostracized by his own appearance, with the mark of Cain definitely upon him. Why not equip these men with a suit of clothes and a pair of shoes that will not reveal the fact that they have but shortly before been discharged from the penitentiary? I have spoken to men who have expiated their crimes, and that is one thing they have asked for above everything else, the opportunity of going out into society without being branded by their appearance.
I have taken occasion, as hon. members in all parts of the house have, to read in Hansard the debates during the last fifteen years dealing with the question of penitentiary reform. The hon, member for Broad view (Mr. Church) throughout the years has made a great contribution and has repeatedly asked that the grand jury have the opportunity and privilege of visiting penal institutions on each occasion prior to the assizes. The grand jury does not exist in many parts of our country, but there should be some form of inspection.
Over the years the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) has made his contribution, and as I read the records I think of one who, over the years, made her contribution. She is no longer a member of this house. I refer to Miss Agnes MacPhail. All these members, and many others who are here today but who were not here ten or fifteen years ago, have made their contributions.

Penitentiary Act
Never was I more impressed with the necessity of there being some form of inspection than by the information which I have received in recent weeks regarding one Canadian institution which does not come under the control of the Department of Justice. I am referring to detention institutions. If the information brought to my attention in respect of one of these is in accordance with the facts it deserves the earliest possible inspection by a man like the gentleman who now presides over the penitentiary service. I refer to Nacnab island near Halifax. It is a naval and army detention institution. The information I have received reveals depressing stories of severity which deserve inspection and consideration by our penail authorities. I should like to see this institution inspected by General Gibson. He should be allowed to go through the place and interview all those confined there as is the case in the other detention camps. He should be permitted to do it confidentially, so that each individual will feel free to report on the conditions that he wishes to report on without having his identity revealed by the fact that he was interviewed by General Gibson.
There was a matter mentioned the other day that had to do with a question asked by a most distinguished practitioner at the criminal bar, the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith). In the course of his speech he asked the question whether or not consideration was being given to a law such as is to be found in the state of New York where, after four convictions for a definite type of crime, a man is removed from circulation. To this the minister replied:
The hon. member will find that consideration was given to that recently.
I do not know what the result of the consideration was but, having regard to its operation, I hope the answer was in the negative, although the answer given by the minister would indicate that favourable consideration had been given to it. To accept the necessity for a measure such as that at this time when the work of reformation has not been given a chance and the new plans as set out by General Gibson have not been experimented with, if you like, would be a retrograde and defeatist attitude. It is true that that law is in effect in the state of New York. It is known as the Barnes law. In Britain as well there is a similar law known as the Habitual Offenders Act, but it was brought in only after about twenty-five years of reformation having been undertaken, when it was definitely assured that, so far as
repeaters were concerned, there was no hope of reformation, regardless of what the state might do.
In any event, my reading of Cohen's Criminal Cases in Britain reveals that the court of appeal views with the utmost care the application of that law. I find, too, that when juries come to realize that a conviction for a fourth offence will mean imprisonment for life, or, as in Great Britain, for a period of ten years, they do what they do everywhere in the world when they realize that a law is unfair and unjust; they interpret that law, not in the light of the law, but in the light of their desire to carry out the principles of justice. Regardless of the evidence, they will, in the circumstances, acquit.
If the minister has looked into this question I suggest he will find that now is not the time for such an act. We are twenty-five, thirty-five, forty years behind in Canada in comparison with other parts of the world in the matter of penitentiary administration. In a large proportion of the cases we have failed to provide reformation. I mention the inspection because, after all, inspection shows what can be done. I mentioned that the other evening. But let us first bring in this new system that General Gibson suggests. Then, after a period of ten or fifteen years, if it is found that reformation will not operate in certain cases, consideration might be given to bringing in an automatic life-term forfeiture piece of legislation.
I cannot quite understand why the government saw fit to depart from one of the major recommendations of the Archambault commission, namely, that of a commission of three. On May 3, 1939, the hon. member for Broadview asked the then minister of justice, the late Mr. Lapointe, what action would be taken to appoint a commission under the law in that regard which received royal assent on April 25, 1939. The answer was that it would be constituted in due time. Well, years have gone by. During the war the excuse was that a war was on, and I am not saying that it was not a good excuse. That was the explanation. Then, by an amendment to the Penitentiary Act, we set up a commission to reinvestigate what a commission had already spent a long period of time investigating. It recommended that the royal commission which heard evidence all over Canada and throughout various parts of the world and based its recommendation on a commission of three, should be departed from. I am in agreement with the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Jaenicke) that this is not the time to make such a change. The commission
Penitentiary Act

of three, composed of outstanding men, one of whom is today the Chief Justice of Ontario, trial division, Mr. Chief Justice McRuer, apparently has not changed his mind in that regard. However, the recommendation is to be changed.
I suggest that even yet the government should return to the principle of a three-man commission rather than adopt that of a one-man commission with two assistants, whose work will be of a scientific nature. Some say to me, what difference does it make? The other day the minister asked my hon. friend what difference it would make whether it was a one-man or a three-man commission. What the minister is trying to do is to lay the foundations for a new and better penological system than we have ever had before. With one in charge, in the nature of things he is more or less hampered by the attitude of the department or the minister. With three, there is a division of responsibility. Three are in a position to say, "We are going to carry out what, we think is right. We are being placed in charge and we are going to administer the system." But with one man, the responsibility falls on him; and whatever his views may be and however desirous he may be of carrying out the best system and bringing into effect the latest in scientific penological knowledge that is available, over and above him he has a stratum which he must break through, namely a group of individuals who have been administering the law over the years. All of us, being human, believe that what has been good enough for the last twenty or thirty years should not be changed all at once. I suggest to the minister that he give consideration to that matter and place before the house and the country in the fullest possible way the reason why he has seen fit to depart from a recommendation which has been made by the Archambault commission and which has been generally accepted everywhere in this country by gaol and penitentiary welfare associations, by penitentiary chaplains who are close to the problem, and also by the wardens of the several penitentiaries.
I now pass on to the next phase. One of the recommendations which the hon. member for Davenport has pressed for over the years has been the bringing into effect of the Borstal system. He has visited the great gaols in the United Kingdom. He has studied the operation of the Borstal system. He has added the weight of his authority and experience to the recommendations of the commission. But we are today no nearer having that system than we were in 1938. Of course the reason for that is that under the British
North America Act there is a division of power regarding penological institutions, whereby gaols and reformatories are under provincial jursidiction and penitentiaries are under federal jurisdiction. But the Archambault commission recommended that the Borstal system be brought in. That recommendation must have been made after consultation with the attorneys general of the various provinces. That recommendation could be earned out by agreement between the federal authorities and the provinces. When the minister replies, I think he should frankly tell the house and the country whether he has been in communication with the provincial attorneys general and what has been done in this regard; because it is a matter of only a few years ago when- according to Mr. McRuer, K.C., as he then was, and as I understand the speech that he made-without exception the various provincial authorities were willing that this be carried into effect.
This is one of the matters which should have come before the dominion-provincial conference in any event. If the government or members of the opposition realized that this was a problem, the solution of which would have a bearing on determining the number of votes, more attention would be given to it. Under those circumstances, this would have been a problem which would have come before the dominion-provincial conference. Apparently it never did. It is true that it concerns the welfare of some 3,600 convicts, but they are human beings too. We talk about recidivists and how they keep coming back three, four and five times. But, sir, where the kind of treatment is accorded which can be given by a warden who is moved by humane feelings, the number of recidivists is always greatly reduced.
I personally have had some little experience over the years with regard to criminal jurisprudence, and I have not seen, in my experience, one instance of an individual who was either convicted and sent to the penitentiary or acquitted after being charged, who ever again became involved in the commission of crime. I think it is a matter of the personality of the individual. There is a difference in wardens.
W'hen you take prisoners from one jurisdiction and move them into another, the statistics of the jurisdiction into which they are moved do not show the true facts.
With regard to the Saskatchewan penitentiary, amongst the convicts from those two provinces who have come into that institution there have been few recidivists. When you place dangerous criminals and repeaters in
[Mr. Diefenbakcr. i

Penitentiary Act
those institutions, you not only undermine the discipline of the place, but also destroy the possibility of reform on the part of many with whom the experienced convicts come into contact.
Now is the time to call a dominion-provincial conference in this regard, so that once and for all we may settle this problem, and the dominion may go as far as it can in carrying out, in association with the provinces, the recommendations of the Archambault commission. Unless you bring that system in, you are building from the roof down. While you may be able to build some kind of place in that way, you can never build as you could if you laid a foundation. You are starting in on the superstructure and using the old foundation. But you cannot hope to achieve the results that could be achieved if you started out once and for all today to bring in a system which has been recommended and which has been found successful in other parts of the world. As a matter of fact, the United Kingdom tried this thirty-nine years ago. They brought in a new system. They departed from the Old Testament principle of an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. Cruel and unfair punishments were abolished 100 years ago, but unfairness still continued, and cruelty was perpetrated on prisoners. Then came the new era and the result has been this. There have been few recidivists, and 17,000 individuals who committed the most serious offences against the criminal law of Great Britain have in the last twenty-five years been completely reformed and become first-rate citizens in that country.
I am just advancing suggestions that have come to me as a result of my own small experience. You put a man in jail; he serves his term, and the mark is on him. At the end of his term he comes out, and over the years his record comes up. These men become cowards, fearful of a revelation being made. If they go to an employer, unless they have assistance from some organization, and tell of their prison records, they are under suspicion. If they are discharged from prison and have to report regularly, finally they have to let the employer know. There is no one to care for them after they leave the penal institutions. Sometimes that information being given an employer results in the dismissal of the individual, and he is on his way back to another penal institution because there are few reformative institutions available to him. That brings me to the next point. Our criminal code is, in large measure, outmoded. The last major amendment was in 1892, when codification took place. Punishments totally out of keeping with present-day conditions are still provided. Modern scientific developments in psychology, psychiatry and sociology have no place in the administration or application of the criminal code. The law of insanity is still tire law of 104 years ago. In the report, reference is made to provision for taking mental cases out of the penitentiaries and sending them to mental institutions. That may be so today, but it was not a fact two or three years ago; for in Prince Albert penitentiary there was a criminal with homicidal tendencies, mentally deficient, who the authorities were warned over a considerable period of time was dangerous. He was kept there; the authorities did not pay any attention to the objections raised. Finally he brutally stabbed one of the warders, Mr. Charles Chisholm, who was saved by one of the lifers who was prepared to give his life for the warder. After that a change was made; but I could name a prisoner, though I am not going to, who was found to be mentally deficient and dangerous fifteen years ago, but who is still confined in that institution along wdth the other prisoners.
I suggest that each prisoner, as General Gibson has stated, should be carefully examined and, where there is serious doubt-not assumed doubts-he should be transferred to the care of an institution where psychiatrists will be able to study his case and perhaps bring about a restoration of his mental faculties. In the mental hospital at North Battle-ford great work is being done in that regard. Today when we were speaking of immigration I thought of the man there who, under the leadership of Doctor Nelson, is doing that work. He was a Czech refugee in 1939, and started a system of psychological experimentation. He was educated in Vienna under Freud, and has brought back quite a number to a realization of their wrongdoing and a desire for reformation, through the removal of fears which originally drove them to the commission of crime.
I spoke about a start. I suggest to the minister that the criminal code be amended to provide that no man may be imprisoned by reason of his poverty, because of his inability to pay a fine. I have spoken about this on previous occasions. One sees it regularly. You have seen it in your practice, Mr. Speaker; every member of this house who is a member of the bar has seen cases rvhere fines are imposed with jail terms as
Penitentiary Act

the alternative. An individual who is unable to pay because of poverty is liable to imprisonment, and in many cases suffers imprisonment for this one reason.

I shall not deal with the other matters I had in mind, but I have one other suggestion in that connection. Imprisonment because of inability to pay a fine has been done away with in Great Britain. Let us do away with it in Canada. Failure to pay a fine should not give poverty a compulsory passport to imprisonment. The individual who is imprisoned for some petty offence serves his term and is marked, and from that point many of them start on the downward path on account of the ostracism which is shown to individuals who have suffered incarceration because of the commission of offences. People do not separate the different offences and say, "Well, it was a picayune matter." All they understand is that the individual has served a term.
My concluding words are in reference to the staffs. However well disposed we may all be toward the matter of reformation; whatever our desire may be to improve the administration of criminal law, the work finally will rest upon those charged with that administration. As far as the two commissioners who will operate along with General Gibson are concerned, there should be available outstanding psychologists, penologists or educators. Advances are being made by the provinces. Ontario has made great advances in the last two years under the Hon. Mr. Dunbar. I pay tribute to what has been done in Saskatchewan even in the last few months as a consequence of the momentous report which was made by the Doctor Lay-cock commission in regard to the question of penal reform. We should recruit for these institutions men and women trained in social and penological science. The universities have many students, overseas men who have returned to this country, who would be only too willing to undertake that type of study, if they were given the opportunity. If this plan of reformation is to be set up, and if we do not have the proper personnel, we are again in the position where, while we have the letter of the law, the spirit will not and cannot be carried out.
I am glad that, under the report, consideration is to be given to increasing the salaries of guards. Major consideration should be given to that matter. There may be some who will say, "You advocate cutting expenses, but at the same time you advocate increasing salaries". I have never advocated increases before. I have never preached both ways. But if we are to make the penal institutions of this country worthy of the responsibility which will rest upon them, I submit, first, that we shall have to come back to the system which prevailed prior to the thirties, whereby the employees will be placed under the Civil Service Act.
I know what the arguments against this would be. But these employees want permanency. If the government wants to recruit the best men it will have to meet the rate of salaries. The present system has its shortcomings, in that efficiency is not always the basis upon which appointments are made. First, we should give opportunity to the servicemen of this and the last war, second, a training course should be provided for so as to encourage young men who have been discharged from the armed forces to go into this work. Salaries should be made attractive enough that the best may be recruited, and permanency must be assured.
I wish to thank the house for its consideration in allowing me to do what ordinarily I do not do, namely, go over the forty minutes allowed. I have endeavoured to place these few suggestions before the minister, based as they are on some knowledge of the subject. General Gibson's report is one which shows that he has devoted himself to the responsibility which has been his. It is the place of parliament at this time, when we are making changes in the Penitentiary Act, to go as far as we can to the end that we make it worthy of the challenge which must come to all of us to make those who are discharged from penal institutions reformed individuals, worthy and willing to take their place in the battle of life.
